h1: How to Get Rid of Mice Humanely: Seal Them Out, Trap Quickly, Clean Up Safely
dek: What the evidence says about humane mouse control: why sealing gaps comes first, which traps CDC recommends, and why catch and release, glue boards and poison are the weakest choices.
excerpt: The most humane way to get rid of mice is to seal every gap over 1/4 inch, then remove the mice inside with snap traps. Here is why release, glue and poison rank lower.

quickAnswer.lead: **The most humane way to get rid of mice is to seal every gap larger than 1/4 inch so they cannot get in, then remove the mice already inside with snap traps and clean up safely.** [CDC advises against glue traps and live traps](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/trap-up.html), and the University of California says released house mice can return or are likely to be attacked or die of exposure.
bullets: Mice can fit through a hole the width of a pencil, 1/4 inch (6 millimeters), so that is the gap size to close.
CDC recommends traditional snap traps and says not to use glue traps or live traps.
UC IPM reports that house mice moved as far as a half mile from their home range can navigate back to their nest.
UC IPM says to use enough traps to make the trapping period short and decisive, spaced no more than about 10 feet apart where mice are active.
NPIC says signs of anticoagulant poisoning in an animal can be delayed for up to five days after exposure.
CDC says not to sweep or vacuum droppings; soak them with 1.5 cups of household bleach per gallon of water for 5 minutes instead.

body.text: What is the most humane way to get rid of mice?

The most humane way to get rid of mice is to keep them out, then remove the ones already inside with snap traps. Sealing every opening larger than 1/4 inch harms no animal, and the [University of California's house mouse guide](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7483.html) calls exclusion the most successful and permanent form of house mouse control. No method that removes a mouse already living in your walls is free of harm to that animal, so the practical question is which methods are decisive and which prolong the suffering.

CDC's rodent guidance runs in three steps: [seal up](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/seal-up.html) the entry points, [trap up](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/trap-up.html) the mice inside, and [clean up](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/clean-up.html) safely. This page follows that order and adds what the evidence says about the gentler-sounding alternatives.

Timing matters for the animals. A hole sealed while a mouse is on the wrong side of it shuts that mouse inside the wall, so close the obvious entry points early and finish the last ones once the traps have stopped catching mice. The [complete mouse control guide](/learn/mice) covers the species, signs and health risks this page leaves out, and a separate guide explains [what to do about mice in walls, attics and crawl spaces](/blog/mice-removal), including a mouse that has died out of reach.
What makes a mouse control method humane?

A method is more humane the less time the animal spends in pain or fear, and the more reliably it ends that quickly. None of the sources cited on this page publishes a measured time to death for household traps, so this page does not put a number on it. What the sources do give is enough to rank the options, because the slow and indirect methods are the ones they warn about.

UC IPM: live mice must be removed frequently and humanely euthanized. CDC says not to use live traps.

UC IPM: mice can navigate back from a half mile, and released mice are likely to be attacked, killed or die of exposure.

body.text: How do you seal mice out of a house?

Close every opening about the width of a pencil or larger. [CDC says](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/seal-up.html) a mouse can fit through a hole 1/4 inch (6 millimeters) across, and UC IPM says to eliminate all gaps and openings larger than 1/4 inch, adding that mice can squeeze under a gap 1/4 inch tall or through an opening 3/8 inch wide. A separate guide shows [how small a gap a mouse can use and which walls it can climb](/blog/can-mice-climb-walls).

The material matters as much as the size. CDC says to fill small holes with steel wool and put caulk around it to keep it in place, or use spray foam, and to fix larger holes with lath screen or metal, cement, hardware cloth or metal sheeting.

UC IPM is more cautious about steel wool: it says steel wool pads make good temporary plugs but may rust over time, recommends metal or concrete for cracks in foundations, and says plastic screening, rubber, vinyl, expanding foam, wood and other gnawable materials are ineffective. The two fit together if caulk or foam is only the retainer, the steel wool or metal is the barrier, and a steel wool plug is checked and replaced when it rusts. A guide to [using steel wool against mice](/blog/steel-wool-for-mice) covers grades, packing and where it fails.
CDC lists these places to check:

items: **Inside.** Kitchen cabinets, closets, fireplaces, windows and doors, behind appliances, pipes under sinks, around water heaters and furnaces, air and dryer vents, electrical, water, gas and sewer lines, the attic, the basement, floor drains and the joints where floors meet walls.
**Outside.** Roof rafters, gables, eaves and soffits, windows and doors, the gap between the foundation and the ground, attic and crawl space vents, and the holes where utilities enter.

body.text: Garage doors are one more place to check, and a separate guide shows how to [seal the corner gap on a garage door](/blog/mouse-proof-garage-door-seal-canada).
Are snap traps humane, and how do you use them well?

Snap traps are the best option for mice already inside, because CDC recommends traditional snap traps and the other common choices carry larger welfare problems, covered below. Neither CDC nor UC IPM gives a time to death for a snap trap, so how humane one is in practice depends on how well it is chosen, baited, placed and checked. The settings below come from [UC IPM](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7483.html) and [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/trap-up.html).

items: **Pick a wide trigger plate.** UC IPM reports that mouse traps with a wide trigger plate have higher catch rates, and says to set the trigger lightly so the trap springs easily.

**Use a small dab of bait.** CDC suggests a small amount of chunky peanut butter or mutton fat on the bait pan. UC IPM adds that too much bait lets a mouse remove it without springing the trap, and that the best bait is often food the mice are already eating; [what mice eat](/blog/what-do-mice-eat) explains why.

**Set traps along walls.** CDC says to place them on the floor against the wall with the baited end touching the wall, so the trap forms a T with it, in areas with signs of mice, in closed spaces such as behind appliances and in cabinets, and near places where you think they are getting in, such as attics, basements and crawl spaces.

**Set enough traps, close together.** UC IPM says to use enough traps to make the trapping period short and decisive, spaced no more than about 10 feet apart where mice are active, since house mice seldom venture more than 30 feet from their nest and food. Pairs set 1 to 2 inches apart can increase capture success.
**Check daily.** CDC says to check traps every day and dispose of dead mice immediately, and to keep traps and bait out of reach of children and pets.

body.text: Battery-operated electronic traps are the alternative. UC IPM says they cost considerably more than other traps, that some homeowners, commercial building managers and pest control companies have found they give good house mouse control, and that they need frequent checking so dead mice can be removed. A guide to [mouse traps by type](/blog/mice-traps) compares snap, electronic and multi-catch designs and where to put each.

body.title: A mouse that is still alive in a trap
body.text: Do not leave an injured mouse to suffer, and do not drown it; UC IPM says drowning is not considered humane. Wear gloves, keep your hands away from the animal, and call a veterinarian or your local animal control office right away for advice on ending its suffering.
Is catch and release a humane way to get rid of mice?

Usually not, because a released house mouse tends to come back or to meet a worse end. CDC says not to use live traps, and UC IPM reports that house mice removed from their home ranges by as much as a half mile can navigate back to their nest. In a new place, UC IPM says released house mice are likely to experience aggression from other mice, be attacked and killed by a predator, or die from exposure if they cannot find shelter.

CDC's stated reason is health rather than welfare: trapped mice can be frightened into urinating, which CDC says can increase your chance of getting sick. The [CDC hantavirus page](https://www.cdc.gov/hantavirus/about/index.html) says people get hantavirus from contact with rodents, especially their urine, droppings and saliva, and names the deer mouse as the source of the most common hantavirus that causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in the United States. A live wild mouse is not an animal to handle with bare hands.

Release can also be against the law. UC IPM states that in California it is illegal to relocate live wildlife, including house mice, away from the property where it was caught without a special permit from the state Department of Fish and Wildlife. Other states differ, and none of the sources used here surveys state rules, so check with your state wildlife agency before releasing any trapped animal. UC IPM also describes what is likely rather than reporting a measured survival rate, and no source cited here gives one.

Multi-catch live traps do not avoid the decision. UC IPM says live mice in them must be removed frequently and humanely euthanized, so the trap becomes a holding device and the decision about the animal's death has only been postponed.
Why are glue traps and poison the least humane options?

Both are slow, and both can harm animals that were never the target. On glue boards, UC IPM says adult rodents can often detect and avoid the glue, so the boards catch mostly juveniles, and that rodents stuck on a board might not die quickly and will need to be euthanized. UC IPM also says drowning a trapped mouse is not considered humane, even though some trap makers suggest it, and that a non-target animal caught on a board can usually be freed by loosening the glue with vegetable oil. CDC advises against glue traps for the same health reason it gives for live traps.

Anticoagulant baits work by causing internal bleeding. [NPIC explains](https://npic.orst.edu/factsheets/rodenticides.html) that these poisons stop an enzyme that recycles vitamin K, which blood clotting needs, and that internal bleeding may begin once the supply runs out. The multiple-dose types need the animal to eat bait over several days, NPIC lists difficulty breathing, weakness and lethargy as signs seen in poisoned animals, with bleeding from the gums and bruising among the less common ones, and it says signs may be delayed for up to five days after exposure. UC IPM likewise says rodenticide baits generally take several days to give effective control.

The harm can travel. NPIC says secondary poisoning happens when an animal eats poisoned prey, and that residues of single-dose anticoagulants can stay in liver tissue for many weeks, so a predator can build up a toxic dose over time. UC IPM adds that there is evidence bromethalin can pass through the food chain to predators. For the active ingredients, the federal rules on consumer products and what to do after an exposure, see the guide to [mouse poison](/blog/mice-poison).
How do you clean up after mice safely?

Wet droppings and nests with disinfectant; never sweep or vacuum them. CDC says sweeping or vacuuming rodent urine, droppings or nesting material can put tiny droplets carrying viruses into the air. These are the steps on [CDC's cleanup page](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/clean-up.html):

items: Open all doors and windows for 30 minutes before you start, and stay out of the area during that time.
Mix 1.5 cups of household bleach into 1 gallon of water (CDC also describes this as 1 part bleach to 9 parts water), or use a disinfectant and follow its label.
Spray droppings, nests and urine until they are very wet, and let them soak for 5 minutes or as long as the disinfectant label says.

For a dead mouse, spray the animal and the area with disinfectant, put it in a plastic bag with the used trap, seal the bag, place it inside a second bag, and put that in a covered garbage can that is emptied regularly.
Wash your gloved hands with soap and water or disinfectant before taking the gloves off, then wash your bare hands with soap and warm water.

body.text: The [CDC hantavirus page](https://www.cdc.gov/hantavirus/about/index.html) lists fatigue, fever and muscle aches as early signs of hantavirus disease, followed by coughing and shortness of breath, and says anyone who suspects it should see a physician immediately and mention the rodent exposure. To confirm what you are cleaning up, see [what mouse droppings look like](/blog/what-does-mouse-poop-look-like-canada). The full method for attics, vehicles and dead mice is in the [guide to mice removal and cleanup](/blog/mice-removal).
How do you keep mice from coming back?

Keep the seals in good repair and take away what draws mice to the property. UC IPM warns that cleaning and decluttering will seldom completely control house mice on their own, though poor sanitation can attract them and lets them thrive in greater numbers, so food control supports exclusion rather than replacing it. CDC's [seal-up guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/seal-up.html) adds these steps:

items: Store food in containers with tight lids.
Put pet food away after use, and do not leave food or water bowls out overnight.
Use a thick plastic or metal garbage can with no holes and a tight lid.
Keep compost bins at least 100 feet from the house.
Move woodpiles 100 feet or more from the house and raise the wood at least one foot off the ground.

body.text: Repellents are often described as the humane option, but CDC's steps are seal up, trap up and clean up, and a repellent is not one of them. A guide to [mouse repellents by type](/blog/mice-repellent) sets out what the evidence says for each kind, and a separate page asks whether [ultrasonic pest repellers work](/blog/ultrasonic-pest-repellers-do-they-work). New droppings or gnaw marks after you have sealed up suggest that an opening is still there or that a new one has formed.
When should you hire a professional, and what should you ask for?

Hire help when you cannot find or reach the entry points, when mice keep returning after you have trapped, or when the work means attics, crawl spaces or heights. A humane service is defined by what it does about entry points and what it uses inside the house. Ask whether sealing is part of the job, whether it will use snap traps, whether it will avoid glue boards, and whether it plans to place poison, where, and how it will find and remove any dead mice.

A guide to [what a mouse exterminator does, the questions worth asking and how to check a license](/blog/mice-exterminator) walks through the process, and the [mice removal guide](/blog/mice-removal) explains what a professional visit usually includes and which parts you can do yourself.

howTo.name: How to get rid of mice humanely

steps.name: Find the entry points
steps.text: Check inside and outside the house for gaps about the width of a pencil, 1/4 inch or larger, including pipes, vents, utility lines, the foundation and the garage door.

steps.name: Remove easy food and shelter
steps.text: Store food in containers with tight lids, put pet food away overnight, use a lidded garbage can, and keep compost bins and woodpiles at least 100 feet from the house.

steps.name: Seal small holes
steps.text: Pack steel wool into holes about the width of a pencil and put caulk around it so the steel wool stays in place.

steps.name: Cover larger gaps
steps.text: Repair larger openings with hardware cloth, metal sheeting, lath screen or cement, because gnawable materials such as plastic, rubber, wood and expanding foam do not stop mice by themselves.

steps.name: Set snap traps
steps.text: Place enough snap traps with a small dab of bait against the walls where you see droppings, no more than about 10 feet apart, with the baited end touching the wall.

steps.name: Check traps daily
steps.text: Check every trap each day while wearing gloves, and spray, double bag and discard any dead mouse with the used trap in a covered garbage can.

steps.name: Clean up droppings and nests
steps.text: Do not sweep or vacuum; open the windows for 30 minutes, then soak droppings and nests with a bleach solution for 5 minutes while wearing gloves.

steps.name: Finish sealing
steps.text: Once the traps stop catching mice, close any remaining openings so that no mouse is shut inside, and keep watching for new droppings or gnaw marks.

faqs.question: What should I do if a mouse is stuck on a glue trap?
faqs.answer: Call a veterinarian or your local animal control office right away and ask how to end its suffering humanely. UC IPM says mice caught on glue boards might not die quickly and will need to be euthanized, and that drowning is not considered humane. Wear gloves and keep bare hands away from the animal. If a non-target animal such as a pet or wild animal is stuck, UC IPM says vegetable oil used as a solvent can loosen the glue in most cases.

faqs.question: What bait should I put on a snap trap?
faqs.answer: CDC suggests a small amount of chunky peanut butter or mutton fat on the bait pan. UC IPM says the best bait is often food the mice are already eating, and that too much bait can let a mouse take it without springing the trap. UC IPM also notes that peanut butter can pose allergy risks, and that nesting materials such as cotton wool or dental floss can be an effective bait.

faqs.question: How many snap traps do I need?
faqs.answer: UC IPM gives no fixed number. It says to use enough traps to make the trapping period short and decisive, spaced no more than about 10 feet apart where mice are active, because house mice seldom venture more than 30 feet from their nest and food. Pairs of traps set 1 to 2 inches apart can increase capture success. CDC says to check traps every day and dispose of dead mice immediately.

faqs.question: Will mice come back after I get rid of them?
faqs.answer: They can if any opening or food source remains. UC IPM calls exclusion the most successful and permanent form of house mouse control and says cleaning and decluttering alone will seldom completely control house mice. CDC's prevention steps include filling holes with steel wool and caulk or with metal, storing food in tight containers, putting pet food away at night, using a lidded garbage can, and keeping compost bins and woodpiles 100 feet or more from the house.

faqs.question: What do I do with a dead mouse from a trap?
faqs.answer: Wear rubber or plastic gloves. CDC says to spray the dead mouse and the area around it with disinfectant, put it in a plastic bag along with the used trap, seal the bag, and place it inside a second plastic bag. Then put the bag in a covered garbage can that is emptied regularly. Wash your gloved hands before removing the gloves, and wash your bare hands with soap and warm water afterward.
